idiom_name: MVVM: dumb XAML view + view model with ICommand and INotifyPropertyChanged, tested by xUnit
implementation_notes: The .NET guidance documents MVVM as the way to keep UI logic testable: the view is defined in XAML with a code-behind that only assigns BindingContext, while the view model exposes properties and ICommand members that the view binds to and that xUnit tests exercise without instantiating a UI type. What replaces the classic humble class is the framework's data binding: commands and bindings are the seam, and INotifyPropertyChanged (with ObservableCollection for lists) is how the humble view learns about changes. Hand-written code-behind is still justified for behaviour XAML cannot express (animations, platform gestures), but any decision that affects state or availability belongs in the view model, bound through IsEnabled or a command's CanExecute.
pitfalls: Code-behind creep: enabling or disabling controls in the view bypasses the view model's CanExecute and makes the behaviour untestable; bind IsEnabled to a view-model property instead, as the MAUI guidance recommends.
Raising PropertyChanged in the middle of an update exposes partially updated state to bound controls, and raising it in the constructor is pointless because the view has not subscribed yet.
A view model that holds Context, handlers or other platform lifecycle objects both leaks and cannot be constructed in a unit test; keep lifecycle objects out of it and pass only what the logic needs.
